### Echidna: a Bayesian framework for integrative inference of copy number alterations impacting phenotypic plasticity
- Nature Methods | 2026-11-16 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-026-03279-4
- First: Joy Linyue Fan | Last: Elham Azizi (Department of Biomedical Engineering, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.; Irving Institute for Cancer Dynamics, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.; )
- Tags: core, disease | n_authors: 18
The ability of cells to adapt their behavior in response to genetic or environmental changes is a fundamental biological process that drives cellular diversity in both normal and pathological contexts, including in tumor evolution. Copy number alterations (CNAs), which can include large-scale changes in genomic ploidy, play a key role in creating adaptive advantages in evolving cell populations. However, tracing these populations across experiments and disentangling the role of CNAs from other sources of transcriptional variability remains challenging and expensive. Here we present Echidna, a Bayesian hierarchical model that integrates single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk whole-genome sequencing data to enable robust integrative inference of CNAs, jointly across samples and treatment time points, to better understand the impact of genomic events on cellular phenotype. Applying Echidna to patient tumor specimens, we demonstrate its superior performance in clonal reconstruction and derive insights into therapy resistance mechanisms.

### Joint single-cell capture of Cas9 edits and transcriptomes reveals on- and off-target effects on gene expression
- Nature Methods | 2026-11-16 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-026-03319-z
- First: Michael H. Lorenzini | Last: Graham McVicker (Integrative Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies, La Jolla, CA, USA. gmcvicker@salk.edu.)
- Tags: core, secondary | n_authors: 9
A longstanding barrier in genome engineering with CRISPR-Cas9 has been the inability to measure editing outcomes and their functional effects at single-cell resolution. Here we present Superb-seq, which captures single-cell edits and transcriptome effects by integrating Cas9 editing, T7 in situ transcription and single-cell RNA sequencing. We performed Superb-seq on 35,000 cells from three cell lines. Using seven guide RNAs to target four chromatin remodeler genes in 10,000 K562 cells, Superb-seq detected 5,761 edited cells, all on-target sites and 36 off-target sites. Superb-seq improved estimation of downstream perturbation effects on gene expression compared to Perturb-seq. We compared Superb-seq to 4 bulk off-target detection methods and identified between 6 and 210 edit sites across 3 benchmarking guides. Nineteen off-target edits were associated with differential gene expression, nine of which were cell type-specific. In summary, Superb-seq illuminates the consequences of Cas9 genome editing by connecting single-cell edits with changes in gene expression.

### A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo
- Nature Biotechnology | 2026-11-16 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-026-03344-5
- First: Lingjuan Hong | Last: Lupeng Ye (Institute of Modern Biology, Department of Hematology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China. lupeng.ye@nju.edu.cn.; State Key Laboratory of Pharmaceutical Biotechnology, Nan)
- Tags: secondary, disease | n_authors: 20
Abstract Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455–457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100–1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

### Principles and assumptions underlying domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
- Nature Genetics | 2026-11-16 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-026-02812-7
- First: Pratibha Panwar | Last: Shila Ghazanfar (School of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Sydney, Camperdown, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. shila.ghazanfar@sydney.edu.au.; Sydney Precision Data Science Centre, The University of )
- Tags: core | n_authors: 15
Spatial-omics technologies simultaneously measure feature expression and locations within tissues, providing an unprecedented opportunity to study tissue structures. The first key step in analyzing these high-dimensional datasets is identifying biologically relevant clusters, yet the large number of spatial-omics clustering (SOC) methods makes method selection challenging. Here we comprehensively review 47 SOC methods and extract information on 108 variables across 26 groups of method characteristics and applicability. This revealed substantial diversity in the underlying algorithms, affecting the suitability of methods to different tissues and biotechnologies. Based on this, we provide an analytical decision tree to help data analysts select methods based on their data types and research questions, and we highlight knowledge gaps to help bioinformaticians identify new avenues for method development. We thus hope to pave the way for more effective applications in a diverse methodological landscape and guide future method development.

### The Drosophila melanogaster Genetic Reference Panel version 3
- Cell Genomics | 2026-11 | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101399
- First: Richard F. Lyman | Last: Trudy F.C. Mackay (Institute for Human Genetics, Greenwood SC 29646 and Department of Genetics and Biochemistry, Clemson University, Clemson, SC 29634, USA. Electronic address: tmackay@clemson.edu.)
- Tags: secondary | n_authors: 12
Drosophila melanogaster is a leading animal model for biomedical research and quantitative, population, and evolutionary genetics and genomics. The D. melanogaster Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP), containing ∼200 inbred strains with full genome sequences, is a publicly available resource for genome-wide association (GWA) analyses of quantitative traits, systems genetics, and population genomic analyses. Here, we describe the DGRP version 3 (DGRP3), consisting of full genome sequences from >1,000 inbred lines. The DGRP3 harbors extensive genetic diversity, with 8,760,339 molecular polymorphisms including single-nucleotide polymorphisms, insertions, deletions, inversions, tandem duplications, and complex rearrangements. We identified putative damaging variants, loss-of-function genes, and mitochondrial haplotype groups and quantified the microbial composition and numbers of sensory bristles for the DGRP3 lines. We performed GWA analyses for host control of the microbiome composition and sensory bristle numbers, identifying candidate variants and genes for each. The accompanying online tool implements GWA mapping for users' DGRP3 data.

### Condensates increase the frequency of transcription
- Molecular Cell | 2026-11 | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.034
- First: Mikayla Eppert | Last: Benjamin R. Sabari (Laboratory of Nuclear Organization, Cecil H. and Ida Green Center for Reproductive Biology Sciences, Division of Basic Research, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Department of Molecular Biolog)
- Tags: core | n_authors: 8
While biomolecular condensates have been implicated in activating transcription, investigating the specific contributions of condensates relative to soluble proteins has been challenging. Here, we leverage the concentration dependence of condensate formation to compare the transcriptional activity of condensed and soluble MYOCD, a cell-type-specific transcriptional coactivator. Using single-cell resolution measurements, we find that cells with MYOCD condensates have more target gene transcripts than cells with soluble MYOCD. While transcription can occur in the absence of condensates, it is less frequent and produces fewer transcripts. Both the frequency of active cells and transcriptional output per cell within a heterogeneous population increase sharply above concentration thresholds that promote condensate formation. Mutants that alter the concentration threshold for condensate formation correspondingly shift the MYOCD concentration at which transcription increases. We propose that condensates enhance transcription by coordinating the multiple steps required for gene activation, making an otherwise infrequent event more common.

### The NADHX epimerase NAXE governs PARP1-DNA retention to maintain poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation homeostasis
- Molecular Cell | 2026-11 | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.033
- First: Yundong Xiong | Last: Jiadong Wang (Department of Gastrointestinal Translational Research, Peking University Cancer Hospital, Department of Radiation Medicine, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Peking University International Cancer Ins)
- Tags: secondary | n_authors: 17
PARP1 is a crucial enzyme involved in DNA-damage repair and other biological processes through poly(ADP-ribose) modification (PARylation), but persistent activation can trigger parthanatos. Despite extensive research, the precise mechanisms governing PARP1 activity remain elusive. Here, through multiple CRISPR-Cas9 screens, we identified NAXE, an NADH hydrate (NADHX) epimerase, as a key regulator of PARP1 activity homeostasis. We show that NADHX inhibits PARP1-DNA binding, while NAXE lowers NADHX levels to promote PARP1 recruitment and DNA repair. PARP1 activation, in turn, induces PARylation that binds and inhibits NAXE, forming a negative feedback loop that restrains PARP1 aberrant activation. Notably, knockout of NAXE in mice and C. elegans disrupts PARylation homeostasis, leading to sustained DNA damage and PARP1 activation, ultimately resulting in parthanatos-driven catastrophic neural injury. These findings uncover a metabolite-mediated feedback mechanism that preserves PARylation homeostasis and highlight NAXE as a potential therapeutic target in PARP1-related neurological disorders.

### An image-based CRISPR screen reveals RNA processing control of HP1α condensates
- Molecular Cell | 2026-11 | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.027
- First: Matthew Man-Kin Wong | Last: Serena Sanulli (Department of Genetics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA. Electronic address: ssanulli@stanford.edu.)
- Tags: secondary | n_authors: 19
Heterochromatin protein 1α (HP1α) is a core component of heterochromatin, forming subnuclear condensates whose regulation and function remain poorly understood. Although RNA has been implicated in heterochromatin organization, how RNA influences HP1α localization remains unclear. Here, we develop an image-based CRISPR screening platform to systematically identify regulators of HP1α condensates and identify RNA processing as a central pathway. Perturbations that disrupt RNA processing increase HP1α-RNA interactions and reduce its association with chromatin, leading to loss of silencing. These findings establish RNA processing as a post-transcriptional mechanism that regulates HP1α localization and heterochromatin by altering the composition and nuclear distribution of HP1α-associated RNAs. More broadly, our work reveals functional crosstalk between RNA processing and chromatin organization, providing a framework for how RNA metabolism can influence nuclear architecture and gene regulation.

### Dissecting the molecular machinery of CRISPR-associated transposons
- Molecular Cell | 2026-11 | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2026.10.035
- First: Shukun Wang | Last: Leifu Chang (Department of Biological Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA; Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA. Electronic address: lchang1)
- Tags: secondary | n_authors: 4
CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) are naturally occurring mobile genetic elements that combine programmable RNA-guided DNA recognition with transposase-mediated integration, enabling site-selective insertion of kilobase-scale DNA without nuclease-induced double-strand breaks. Current structural and biochemical knowledge can be viewed in terms of three functional modules: the transposase module, which performs DNA cleavage and strand transfer; the AAA+ ATPase TnsC, which forms a recruitment and regulatory platform; and TnsD or CRISPR effector-TniQ targeting complexes, which position this platform at selected DNA sites. Here, we synthesize recent structural and biochemical advances in target recognition, recruitment, donor-end pairing, and strand transfer. Comparisons with Tn7 and phage Mu highlight conserved transposase and ATPase functions and system-specific differences in how these components are organized and regulated. We discuss the implications of these advances for engineering programmable DNA-insertion systems and highlight unresolved questions in CAST transposition.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) plasma biomarkers are cost-effective tools to detect early stage amyloid pathology. We investigated how interactions between AD genetic risk (apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4, AD polygenic risk score (excluding APOE; PRSAD)), age, and sex affected AD plasma biomarkers concentrations in a population-based cohort. We included 5913 participants from the Netherlands Twin Register age 30 - 80 (64.1% females, 29.8% ε4 carriers) and measured plasma phosphorylated-tau-217 (p-tau217), amyloid-β-42/40 (Aβ-42/40), neurofilament light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). We showed that the PRSAD did not associate with biomarker concentrations over age. In ε4 carriers, decreases in Aβ-42/40 became steeper after age 50, and increases in p-tau217 and GFAP became steeper after age 55 and 60 compared to non-carriers, respectively. These results highlight the potential of plasma biomarkers, especially p-tau217, for early detection of preclinical AD pathology.

Periodicity is ubiquitous in genomic data. Assembled sequences are dense with homopolymers, microsatellites, and large satellite arrays, which contribute to phenotype, variation, and disease. Third-generation sequencing technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore (ONT) and PacBio HiFi, has enabled longer and increasingly accurate reads, but have brought with them systematic error biases in repetitive regions, where insertions and deletions can distort array lengths and mimic or obscure biological variation. This periodicity is not benign: local repetitiveness makes sequence alignment ambiguous and genome assembly error-prone. In sequence analysis, these two manifestations of periodicity are simultaneously at play, each compounding the challenges of the other; a unified representation of repetitive and non-repetitive sequence is necessary to account for their combined effects consistently. We propose a paradigm under which (either repetitive and non-repetitive) DNA is split into its identity (its irreducible components) and its geometry (how its components are realized). Endogenous single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs) that arise during active DNA demethylation, regulate neurodevelopmental gene expression. Thymine (TDG) and alkyladenine (AAG) DNA glycosylases recognize oxidized methylcytosines. While TDG is required for excision, role of AAG in active demethylation and neurodevelopment remains unknown. Using mouse neurospheres, hippocampus, and human induced neurons (iNs), we show that AAG is needed for neurogenesis. Loss of AAG contributes to delayed neurodevelopmental and premature synaptic gene expression, evident from single-cell RNA sequencing of differentiating iNs. Synaptic gene expression is co-regulated by both AAG and TDG, with loss of single glycosylase inducing an opposing effect, implying competition. Single-molecule and biochemical assays directly demonstrate this competition, with AAG inhibiting TDG on 5fC. Without AAG, TDG has higher affinity, resulting in reduced global 5fC and increased SSB intermediates. In summary, AAG substrate competition plays an important role in fine tuning active demethylation, thereby regulating gene expression and DNA breaks during neurogenesis.

Our results suggest that use of a second G subunit allows a switch to the degranulation output.

The term 'spatial niche' is widely used in spatial omics analyses but is inconsistently defined across studies. We survey the literature and find that it most commonly refers to the following three distinct concepts: (1) a proximity-based neighborhood around an anchor cell or spatial spot; (2) a computationally derived spatial domain comprising spatially proximal spots or cells with shared molecular features; and (3) a biologically grounded ecosystem comprising cellular and noncellular components that support resident cells. We organize existing studies under this taxonomy and distinguish two main analytical roles-niches as spot-level covariates for modeling local context, and niches as spot clusters for within-niche and between-niche compositional and molecular analyses.
